articles.title: In Europe, Too, Amazon’s Warehouses Are a Dystopia
articles.author: Li Andersson
articles.content_excerpt: When you see it, it’s hard to believe that nobody, at any point from planning to installation, raised a hand to say how tone-deaf it was. But there it is, emblazoned in bright colors above the gates where workers enter an Amazon warehouse in Germany: “Work hard. Have fun. Make history.” The corporate Americana and hyperoptimistic bravado are enough to make us wince. In Germany, of all places, words about work above an iron gate also bring to mind a much darker time and another slogan about work and freedom. It’s a terrible look. That gate was our introduction to a fact-finding mission to Amazon warehouses in Germany and Poland. Once a year, the whole island of Bali goes silent for a day. Nyepi, the Balinese Hindu New Year, shuts the island down completely, airport included, and no hotel concierge can talk anyone onto a plane. Democracy can be messy, but one thing should be simple: If you win the most votes, you should win the election. Unfortunately, when it comes to the highest office in the United States, that’s not always the case. But after the latest election results, we may be closer than ever to fixing this egregious flaw in our democracy. To elect presidents, we rely on the Electoral College . Rather than a national popular vote, the Electoral College decides the presidential election by counting “electoral votes” allocated to states. articles.title: In Spain, the Indignados’ Parties Are Dwindling Fast
articles.author: Carlos Delclós
articles.content_excerpt: On September 23, Maricarmen Abascal was carried on a stretcher out of her apartment in the Retiro district of Madrid, where she’d been living since 1956. She was eighty-seven, disabled, and had limited mobility. Neighbors and members of the Madrid Tenants’ Union had formed a human chain to stop the eviction. This time, the police broke through it. As she was carried out, the crowd shouted that she was not alone. Two weeks later, she died in a hospital, before she could return to her home, under an agreement with her corporate landlords that arrived far too late. Her case set off a massive wave of mobilization led by a confederation of tenants’ unions.
